generated_by: prism-parity:tools/generate-thread-rows.php for php; tools/record-thread-rows.mjs for ts and tools/record_thread_rows.py for py. Every output is execution output, encoded as compact JSON with keys in the order each language wrote them.
pins_note: The rows a harness stores for a run, and what a stored run is replayed as. A PHP app and a TypeScript or Python agent can share one session. If they store tool calls, approvals or decisions in different shapes, one language resumes the other’s approval against the wrong call or never, or replays a conversation a provider refuses.

cases.title: a reply with no tool calls and no provider state
cases.notes: The control, and the empty-map boundary. A reply with no provider state must store an EMPTY MAP, not an empty list: a reader in a typed language that expects an object refuses a list, and PHP writes an empty array as a list unless told otherwise.

cases.title: a tool call with its arguments, provider ids and provider state
cases.notes: G-58. Everything the next request has to send back: the call's arguments (a tool_use without input is refused), OpenAI's call and reasoning ids, and Anthropic's thinking signature. The ports used to store an id and a name only.

cases.title: a tool call with NO arguments
cases.notes: The empty-arguments boundary. `arguments` must be an empty map. Stored as an empty list, it is replayed to a provider as an array where an object is required, and the request is refused.

cases.title: two calls waiting on approval, one approval request each
cases.notes: G-59. The approval requests ride on the assistant row, each naming the call it authorises. A language that stored them elsewhere, or keyed them differently, would resume a PHP-recorded approval against the wrong call or never, and an approved call must never run as the wrong one.

cases.title: arguments a hostile model chose
cases.notes: Adversarial arguments stored as data, never interpreted: an injection string, a `__proto__` key that must stay an ordinary key, a dotted key that must not become a path, non-ASCII text, an empty string, and a traversal-shaped path. All three languages must store exactly what the model sent.

cases.title: all of a step's results in one row
cases.notes: One row per step, as the reference stores it, with each result keyed by its call. A result that looks like JSON stays a string and must not be decoded into structure. The empty-arguments boundary again, on `args`.

cases.title: decisions only: an approval, a denial with a reason, a denial without one
cases.notes: What recording a decision writes. A denial must stay a denial across languages: an `approved` that became truthy, or a missing reason that became an empty string, changes what the resumed run does. Refused calls never run.

cases.title: a stopped step, its decision and the resumed results, replayed as one
cases.notes: G-59. An approval leaves three consecutive tool result rows. Replayed separately, a provider receives the search output twice, and Anthropic receives an empty user turn for the decision-only row, which it refuses. Folded, each call has one result and each approval one decision.

cases.title: a later row replaces an earlier result and decision in the earlier position
cases.notes: The order a fold keeps when the same call or approval appears twice: the later value wins, in the position the first one had. If languages disagreed, the same stored thread would show a model a different result, or a spoofed later decision, in PHP than in TypeScript.

cases.title: tool result rows with a turn between them are not folded
cases.notes: The boundary of a fold: only CONSECUTIVE rows merge. Merging across a turn would move a result away from the call it answers, and providers must never be sent a result before its call.

cases.title: a structured answer: the document as text, the parsed object beside it
cases.notes: A structured turn stores the document AS THE ASSISTANT MESSAGE'S TEXT, with the parsed object beside it under `structured`, alongside whatever provider state the turn carried. Storing the object instead would make the row unreadable to every reader that handles text -- which is every reader a thread already has. Pins that the parsed document is metadata, that it sits next to provider state rather than replacing it, and that a nested list inside it stays a list in all three.

cases.title: a REFUSED structured answer is recorded, with a null document

input.content: I am afraid I cannot help with that.

rows.php: [{"type":"assistant","content":"I am afraid I cannot help with that.","tool_calls":[],"additional_content":{"structured":null},"tool_approval_requests":[]}]
rows.ts: [{"type":"assistant","content":"I am afraid I cannot help with that.","tool_calls":[],"additional_content":{"structured":null},"tool_approval_requests":[]}]
rows.py: [{"type":"assistant","content":"I am afraid I cannot help with that.","tool_calls":[],"additional_content":{"structured":null},"tool_approval_requests":[]}]

cases.notes: The exchange happened, so it is in the thread even though the run failed: a thread that omits the answer it did not like cannot explain the retry sitting next to it. The boundary is the null -- a key present and null is different bytes from a key that is absent, and a language that dropped it would leave a reader unable to tell a refused structured turn from an ordinary reply.

cases.title: a structured row replays as an ordinary assistant message
cases.notes: What the NEXT turn sends. The document reaches the provider as the text the model wrote, and the parsed object rides along untouched -- a transcript that differed by the shape of the request that produced it is the defect the streaming path already refuses to have. A language that promoted `structured` into the content, or dropped it on replay, would send a different conversation than the other two.

cases.notes: G-387: a runner start never acts on a decision recorded on the child; it ends the calls the child was parked on with its task row, each with one fixed result, and marks the row with the approvals they were asked under. That mark is the ONLY thing that makes an ended call read ended, so it is pinned here byte for byte: `harness_ended_by_start` as a top-level key AFTER `tool_approval_responses`, never inside a result (a tool controls its result text, never this key), holding `{approval_ids: [...]}` in CALL order, not in the order the requests were stored (the requests here are deliberately reversed). The two calls carry DISTINCT tool_call ids; calls that share one id are G-392's and are not in this row. A language that wrote another shape, or none, would read a call another language ended as approved, the decision standing for a side effect that never ran.

cases.title: which approvals read ended when a step repeats a call id and an earlier result row carries it

tool_approval_responses.reason: Tool call was not run because another call in this step has the same id

tool_results.result: Not run: the delegation this call was proposed under ended.

cases.notes: G-387 round 13: the READ rule for the ended mark. An approval reads ended by a runner start when ANY result row after the assistant row that asked for it, and before the next assistant row, carries `harness_ended_by_start` naming its approval id; nothing else ends it. apr_1 was asked on a step whose two calls share the id `dup`: the ungated echo ran first and its row (no mark) carries `dup`, then the person's decision, then the start's marked row. A reader that stopped at the FIRST result row carrying the call id read apr_1 as not ended, so the decision stood for a call that never ran. apr_0's own step ended at the next assistant row, so a mark naming it after that row does not end it, and apr_9 was never asked. The output is one entry per id in `approvals`, in that order: `{approval_id, ended_by_start}`.

cases.notes: G-403 (G-387 round 14). The replay keys a result by its tool call id, tool name AND recorded arguments, never by the call id alone: a provider may give two calls of one step the same id. The step's ungated echo ran at once, the gated weather call was denied as a repeated-id step, and the resolution row carries both results again. Folded, the replay holds BOTH results once each, in call order, and the decision once. A fold keyed by id alone kept one of the two, so the model was not shown the output of a tool that ran.

cases.title: a step's results recorded after a system row are replayed once, in the step's own rows
cases.notes: G-387 round 14, item 5. A step's segment is every row after it up to the next assistant row with tool calls, and its result rows need not be consecutive: a system row leaves the step parked, and the resolution recorded after it carries the step's earlier results again. The replay emits each result (tool call id, tool name and arguments, occurrence by occurrence) and each decision ONCE per segment: the first stands where it was, a later run of the segment leaves out what an earlier run already replayed, and a run left with nothing is not replayed. Here call_1's result is replayed once, before the system row, and call_2's once, after it. A fold of consecutive rows alone replayed call_1 twice, which a provider can refuse as a duplicate tool result.

divergence_note: thr-0001..thr-0013 agree across PHP, TypeScript and Python. thr-0016 and thr-0017 (0.5.0) pin the replay fold for same-id calls and for a step whose result rows are not consecutive; the ports agree once they fold by id, tool name and arguments, once per segment. thr-0015 (0.4.0) pins how the ended mark is READ on a step whose call ids repeat; it agrees once each port reads every result row of the step, not only the first that carries the call id. thr-0014 (0.3.0) pins the ended mark, which the three languages wrote in three different shapes before it; it agrees once each port records the PHP reference's row. Seven did not on the first run: the reference stored an empty provider state as an empty list, [], where the ports store an empty map, {}, and the reference moved. Agreement here means a run stored by one language has the same rows, and replays as the same messages, in the others. It does not mean the decisions in those rows were authorised. User rows are out of scope here by decision; a draft of thr-0013 that carried them found PHP writing additional_content and additional_attributes as empty LISTS where both ports write neither key, recorded under G-58 rather than pinned in a suite that says it does not cover them.
